intro: Read the deck for the facts and these notes for the thinking. Each note under a slide explains why it matters, how to remember it and where people slip. Work the exercises in pencil, test yourself with the recall questions, and write your own notes in the margins beside mine.

sections.title: What counts as aid
sections.big_idea: Official aid passes **three tests**: official, developmental and concessional. Everything else, however large, is counted elsewhere.
in_plain_words: Most development work in South Asia runs on someone else's money, and each source brings its own rules and idea of success. Official development assistance is the standard measure: a flow from government to an eligible country or multilateral agency, aimed mainly at development, on concessional terms. A private foundation grant fails the first test however large it is.

The boundary matters because governments are judged by their ODA totals. Military aid and near-market loans are classed as other official flows. Loans now count at their grant equivalent, and the 0.7 per cent target dates from 1970. **Only four donors met it in 2025**, so read any aid statistic with four checks: gross or net, current or constant, flows or grant equivalent, preliminary or final.

worked_example.title: Does a loan count as ODA?
worked_example.setup: A donor lends US$100 million with a 40 per cent grant element. Use the deck's thresholds: 45 per cent for least developed and other low-income countries, 15 for lower middle-income, 10 for upper middle-income.
steps: Grant equivalent counted: 100 × 40 ÷ 100 = 40, so US$40 million in the year it is signed.
To a lower middle-income country the threshold is 15, and 40 is above it, so it counts.
To a least developed country the threshold is 45, and 40 is below it, so it is classed as OOF.
Repayments in later years do not reduce ODA.
worked_example.answer: US$40 million of ODA if lent to a lower middle-income country, and OOF if lent to a least developed country.

mistakes: Counting a private foundation grant as ODA because it is large.
Comparing ODA totals across 2018 or 2019 without allowing for the grant-equivalent change.
Quoting an aid number without saying whether it is net or gross, current or constant.
Treating the 0.7 per cent target as an estimate of need, when it was a political compromise.

recall.q: Name the three tests for ODA.
recall.a: Official, developmental as the main objective, and concessional.

recall.q: Which four DAC members exceeded 0.7 per cent in 2025?
recall.a: Norway, Luxembourg, Sweden and Denmark.

recall.q: What did the DAC give as a share of GNI in 2025?
recall.a: 0.26 per cent, down from 0.34 per cent in 2024.

recall.q: Why is military assistance not ODA?
recall.a: Its main aim is not development, so it is classed as other official flows.

recall.q: Name the four checks for an aid statistic.
recall.a: Gross or net, current or constant prices, flows or grant equivalent, preliminary or final.

sections.title: How aid moves
sections.big_idea: The route and form of aid decide **who controls the money**, and every layer between donor and community takes a share.
in_plain_words: A donor can spend directly through bilateral channels or give to a multilateral body, where a board allocates by formula and need. Many donors earmark money through UN agencies, keeping bilateral control inside a multilateral channel. Humanitarian aid works in weeks and months, development aid over years, and the two run on different rules and budgets.

The form of aid matters as much as the amount. Budget support gives the recipient most control, tied aid sends part of the budget back to donor firms, and project aid gives control to donor and implementer. Aid rarely travels straight to communities: **every layer adds overhead and power**. ODA is also only one flow among several, and for many South Asian economies it is now small.

diagram.caption: each layer adds overhead and holds power over the next

key_terms.meaning: Government to government, or donor agency to NGO.
Core contributions to bodies such as IDA or UNICEF.

worked_example.title: How much can be traced?
worked_example.setup: The deck says two thirds of humanitarian funding, US$17.4 billion, could not be tracked beyond the first recipient.
steps: Two thirds is 17.4, so one third is 17.4 ÷ 2 = 8.7.
Whole funding: 17.4 + 8.7 = 26.1 billion.
The traced part beyond the first recipient: 26.1 − 17.4 = 8.7 billion.
Only about one third of the dollars can be followed past the first recipient.
worked_example.answer: About US$26.1 billion in total, of which only about US$8.7 billion can be traced past the first tier.

mistakes: Treating all aid as one thing, when the form decides who controls spending.
Accepting a tied grant without asking whether you must hire the donor's consultants.
Adding remittances, investment and ODA together as 'aid'.
Assuming the community group receives the donor's full grant.

recall.q: What is multi-bi aid?
recall.a: Money passed through a UN agency but earmarked for a country or theme.

recall.q: Which form gives the recipient government most control?
recall.a: Budget support.

recall.q: What did untying aid appear in?
recall.a: The Paris Declaration commitments of 2005.

recall.q: What happened to humanitarian ODA in 2025?
recall.a: It fell 35.8 per cent, its second year of decline.

recall.q: What made Ukraine's 2025 ODA exceptional?
recall.a: At US$44.9 billion it was the largest volume ever to a single country and exceeded bilateral ODA to all least developed countries.

sections.title: The great aid debate
sections.big_idea: Keep four questions apart: **does aid raise growth, does this programme work, does it change accountability, and do we owe it**.
in_plain_words: The argument over aid is confused because people answer different questions. Sachs argued for a coordinated big push to escape a poverty trap. Easterly contrasted planners with searchers who test, learn and adapt. Moyo argued government-to-government aid reduces a state's need to answer to its citizens.

The cross-country evidence swings with the method, with the problem of reverse causation at the centre. Singer's drowning child gives the ethical case, written in 1971 for refugees from the Bangladesh war. You do not need to settle the macro debate to do good work. **Separate the evidence for the intervention from the evidence for aid in general.**

key_terms.meaning: Being stuck below the bottom rung of the development ladder.
Easterly's contrast between top-down and test-and-adapt actors.
Donors send more aid to countries in trouble, so aid looks harmful.
Does aid raise growth across countries?
Does this intervention change outcomes?
Singer's thought experiment that distance changes no duty.

worked_example.title: Check two numbers from the debate
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's figures. Sachs wanted aid to rise from US$65 billion in 2002 to between US$135 and US$195 billion a year by 2015. Easterly cited about US$2.3 trillion over roughly fifty years.
steps: Upper end of Sachs's range against 2002: 195 ÷ 65 = 3, three times.
Lower end: 135 ÷ 65 = 2.08, about double.
Easterly's average per year, in US$ billion: 2,300 ÷ 50 = 46.
So Sachs's range is above the 46 billion yearly average Easterly describes.
worked_example.answer: Sachs asked for between two and three times the 2002 level, and Easterly's figure averages about US$46 billion a year.

mistakes: Citing a cross-country regression as proof that aid works or fails in general.
Taking Easterly as against all aid, when he accepts targeted health successes.
Treating Moyo's argument as proven, when reviewers faulted her use of evidence.
Using an authors' debate about Africa as if it were about South Asia first.

recall.q: What is Easterly's central contrast?
recall.a: Planners, who set large goals from outside, against searchers, who test, learn and adapt.

recall.q: What did Rajan and Subramanian find in 2008?
recall.a: Little evidence of a positive or negative effect, and no sign that aid works better under better policy.

recall.q: What is the main problem in cross-country aid studies?
recall.a: Reverse causation: donors send more aid to countries in trouble.

recall.q: What did Sen say of Easterly?
recall.a: He praised the attention to incentives but called the rejection of planning too sweeping.

recall.q: What test follows from Singer's essay?
recall.a: If we can prevent something very bad without sacrificing anything of comparable importance, we ought to.

sections.title: The aid effectiveness agenda
sections.big_idea: From Paris to Busan, donors promised **ownership, alignment and accountability**, and mostly missed their own targets.
in_plain_words: After the Millennium Development Goals, donors and recipients met repeatedly to agree how aid should be delivered. The Paris Declaration of 2005 set five principles and measurable targets for 2010. Its monitoring showed real but slow progress, with most targets missed, and the pattern was that targets depending on recipients improved more than those needing donors to change.

Accra added civil society and parliaments, and Busan moved from aid effectiveness to development effectiveness and created a global partnership. The agenda then lost momentum: donors wanted visible results, security and migration drew budgets, and new lenders did not sign up. **The principles still work as a checklist**: a funder who aligns with your plan and reports jointly is following Paris.

key_terms.meaning: 2005 agreement with five principles and 12 indicators.
2008 agenda adding civil society and more predictable aid.
2011 forum that created the Global Partnership (GPEDC).
A donor-funded unit that bypasses ministry systems.
The recipient's own budget, procurement and audit processes.
Countries setting and leading their own development strategies.

worked_example.title: How far did parallel units fall?
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's Paris indicator: 1,696 parallel project implementation units in 2005, a target of 565, and an outcome of 1,158 in 2010.
steps: Fall achieved: 1,696 − 1,158 = 538.
Share of the needed fall: 538 ÷ 1,131 = 47.6%.
Under half of the intended reduction happened, which fits the slide's pattern of donor-side targets lagging.
worked_example.answer: Units fell by 538 of the 1,131 needed, about 47.6 per cent of the intended reduction.

mistakes: Calling the Paris targets met, when only coordinated technical cooperation was.
Assuming ownership means the government is accountable to its citizens.
Forgetting that a pooled fund cannot carry one donor's logo, which is why donors resist it.
Dropping the principles as outdated, when they remain a useful funder checklist.

recall.q: List the five Paris principles.
recall.a: Ownership, alignment, harmonisation, results and mutual accountability.

recall.q: What did Accra add that was most visible?
recall.a: Recognition that civil society and parliaments, as well as governments, should shape development policy.

recall.q: What did Busan create?
recall.a: The Global Partnership for Effective Development Co-operation, replacing the forum process.

recall.q: Which Paris 2010 target was met?
recall.a: Coordinated technical cooperation, with 57 per cent against a target of 50.

recall.q: Name two forces that stalled the agenda.
recall.a: Any two of: visibility, risk, attribution, politics, fragmentation, lower volume.

sections.title: The 2025 aid cuts
sections.big_idea: Aid fell **23.1 per cent in real terms** in 2025, the largest drop on record, led by the United States and joined by every large donor.
in_plain_words: The OECD's preliminary data show DAC aid at US$174.3 billion, down from US$215.1 billion, bringing it back to 2015 levels. The fall is concentrated and broad at once: the United States cut 56.9 per cent and the five largest providers account for 95.7 per cent of the decline, while 26 of 34 members cut.

The US dismantled USAID within six months, starting with a 90-day pause by Executive Order 14169. The UK is moving from 0.5 to 0.3 per cent to pay for defence. A Lancet study estimates the human cost with wide intervals. **The cuts fall hardest where alternatives are fewest**, and many South Asian NGOs felt them as a stop-work notice from a partner.

worked_example.title: Work the 2025 totals
worked_example.setup: Use the OECD figures in the deck: DAC ODA fell from US$215.1 billion in 2024 to US$174.3 billion in 2025. The five largest providers gave 29.1, 29.0, 17.2, 16.2 and 14.5.
steps: Fall in current dollars: 215.1 − 174.3 = 40.8 billion.
As a share of 2024: 40.8 ÷ 215.1 = 19.0%, against 23.1 per cent in real terms.
worked_example.answer: A fall of US$40.8 billion (19.0 per cent nominal), with the five largest giving US$106.0 billion, about 60.8 per cent of the total.

mistakes: Quoting the nominal fall as if it were the real one reported by the OECD.
Treating the Lancet's forecast as a measured result, when it is observational with wide ranges.
Assuming a stop-work only reaches organisations that held a USAID contract.
Relying on FCDO funding without checking the current country allocation.

recall.q: What was the real-terms fall in DAC ODA in 2025?
recall.a: 23.1 per cent, the largest annual drop on record.

recall.q: What did Executive Order 14169 do?
recall.a: Froze new obligations and disbursements of US development aid for 90 days while programmes were reviewed.

recall.q: What is the UK's announced ODA target for 2027, and why?
recall.a: 0.3 per cent of GNI, to help pay for defence spending of 2.5 per cent of GDP.

recall.q: What range does the Lancet study give for extra deaths by 2030?
recall.a: 14.05 million, with a range of 8.5 to 19.7 million.

recall.q: Name two strategic responses for NGOs.
recall.a: Any two of: diversify funders, build domestic and CSR income, keep three to six months of reserves, write exit clauses into sub-grants.

sections.title: Aid to South Asia
sections.big_idea: Look at **three measures** for each country, total, share of income and per person, because they give three different stories.
in_plain_words: World Bank data report net ODA received, meaning disbursements minus repayments of principal. In 2023 Bangladesh received the most in total, Afghanistan the highest share of national income at 17.76 per cent, and India the least per person at US$1.65. India's total is large in rupees but close to zero beside its economy, at 0.07 per cent of GNI.

Totals move a lot from year to year because loans arrive in lumps and repayments return in others, and a net figure can even be negative, as Sri Lanka's was in 2018. High dependence changes bargaining power: a ministry that relies on donors has less room to refuse conditions. **Always show more than one year**, and say whether the figure is gross or net.

diagram.caption: the same data read three ways

key_terms.meaning: Grants and concessional loans disbursed, minus principal repaid.
Aid as a proportion of national income, a measure of dependence.
Aid divided by population, which reverses the country ranking.
Reliance on donors for a large part of public finance.
Net subtracts repayments, so it can be negative.
World Bank World Development Indicators.

worked_example.title: Compare dependence and growth
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's 2023 figures. Nepal's net ODA was 2.82 per cent of GNI and India's 0.07. Bangladesh's net ODA rose from US$2,154 million in 2012 to US$5,684 million in 2023.
steps: Nepal against India: 2.82 ÷ 0.07 = 40.3, about forty times.
Bangladesh growth: 5,684 ÷ 2,154 = 2.64 times.
Illustrative: if Sri Lanka's repayments of principal in a year were US$397 million against new aid of US$150 million, repayments exceed new aid by 397 − 150 = 247.
That would give a net figure of minus 247, as in 2018, a statement about loan timing.
worked_example.answer: Nepal's dependence is about forty times India's, Bangladesh's net aid grew 2.64 times, and a negative net figure means repayments exceeded new aid.

mistakes: Quoting one year's per person figure, when Sri Lanka's moved from US$0.55 to US$37.54 in one year.
Reading a negative net ODA figure as donors withdrawing goodwill.
Treating rising net ODA as more grants, when it may mean more borrowing.
Taking Afghanistan's share of GNI as exact, when crisis-year GNI estimates are uncertain.

recall.q: What does net ODA received mean?
recall.a: Grants and concessional loans disbursed, minus repayments of principal on earlier aid loans.

recall.q: Which South Asian country received the highest share of GNI as aid in 2023?
recall.a: Afghanistan, at 17.76 per cent.

recall.q: How much per person did India and Nepal receive in 2023?
recall.a: US$1.65 for India and US$39.51 for Nepal.

recall.q: Why was Sri Lanka's 2018 net ODA negative?
recall.a: Repayments of principal on earlier concessional loans exceeded the new aid it received.

recall.q: What was Nepal's peak share of GNI and when?
recall.a: 5.2 per cent in 2020, the decade peak.

sections.title: India as a development partner
sections.big_idea: India is **recipient and provider at once**, and its South-South partnership sits outside the ODA statistics.
in_plain_words: India still receives US$2.38 billion in net ODA, yet it also provides development finance and training through the Ministry of External Affairs. It is not a DAC member, so its outgoing assistance follows its own rules. It describes this as development partnership and South-South cooperation, which avoids the hierarchy of donor and recipient.

ITEC has trained partners since 1964. Lines of credit under IDEAS are routed through Exim Bank and pay for Indian goods and services, worth about US$32 billion across 68 countries. **Both claims can be true**: requests come from partners with few conditions, and procurement is tied to Indian suppliers. Data on disbursement and results are thinner than DAC reporting.

left.title: India as recipient
items: World Bank, ADB, Japan, NGO grants

key_terms.meaning: Indian Technical and Economic Cooperation programme, launched 1964.
Scheme for concessional government-backed lines of credit.

Loan routed through Exim Bank to buy goods and services from India.
Development partnership among developing countries.

worked_example.title: Size the lines of credit
worked_example.setup: Use the MEA figures in the deck: US$32 billion across 68 partner countries. Bangladesh accounts for about a quarter. Africa received 196 lines worth US$12 billion.
steps: Bangladesh's share: 32 ÷ 4 = 8, about US$8 billion.
Africa's share of the total: 12 ÷ 32 = 37.5%.
Average per partner country, in US$ million: 32,000 ÷ 68 = 470.6.
Average per African line, in US$ million: 12,000 ÷ 196 = 61.2.
worked_example.answer: About US$8 billion to Bangladesh, 37.5 per cent of the total to Africa, and an average of about US$471 million per partner country.

mistakes: Counting Indian outgoing assistance within DAC ODA totals.
Describing lines of credit as untied, when they buy Indian goods and services.
Expecting an open call for proposals, when projects are negotiated government to government.
Treating the DPA as an independent agency, when it sits inside the foreign ministry.

recall.q: When was ITEC launched?
recall.a: On 15 September 1964, by the Ministry of External Affairs.

recall.q: Why does Indian development partnership sit in the MEA?
recall.a: It is treated as foreign policy, tied to Neighbourhood First and relations with Africa.

recall.q: What do lines of credit pay for?
recall.a: Goods and services from India, including consultancy, on deferred credit terms.

recall.q: Name two criticisms of India's approach.
recall.a: Procurement tied to Indian suppliers, credits adding to partners' debt, or limited public data on results.

recall.q: How does India's reporting differ from DAC donors'?
recall.a: India does not report to the OECD as ODA because it is not a DAC member.

sections.title: Philanthropy in India: money and law
sections.big_idea: Public money is about **95 per cent** of social sector funding, and three laws shape what private money may do: s135, the FCRA and the tax code.
in_plain_words: India's social sector funding is about ₹27 lakh crore, mostly public. Private philanthropy is small by comparison and led by families. Mandatory CSR is a large but minority part of it, and concentrates in industrial states where companies are headquartered, with education and health taking more than half.

Section 135 applies to companies meeting any one of three thresholds and requires 2 per cent of average net profit to be spent on Schedule VII activities, with strict rules for unspent money. The FCRA regulates foreign money, and its 2020 amendment barred transfers to any other person and capped administrative spending at 20 per cent. **Income-tax Act 2025, section 133**, now governs donation deductions.

worked_example.title: Is a company covered, and what must it spend?
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a company had net worth ₹400 crore, turnover ₹1,200 crore and net profit ₹3 crore last year. Its net profit over the last three years was ₹250, ₹300 and ₹350 crore.
steps: The thresholds are net worth ₹500 crore, turnover ₹1,000 crore or net profit ₹5 crore, and any one is enough.
Turnover of ₹1,200 crore is above ₹1,000 crore, so the company is covered.
Total profit over three years: 250 + 300 + 350 = 900.
Required spend at 2 per cent: 300 × 2 ÷ 100 = 6 crore.
worked_example.answer: The company is covered through its turnover and must spend ₹6 crore.

mistakes: Assuming a company needs to pass all three thresholds. Any one is enough.
Counting spending outside Schedule VII, or benefits to the company's own employees, as CSR.
Passing FCRA funds to a partner, which s7 forbids since 2020.
Claiming a tax deduction on a cash donation over ₹2,000.

recall.q: What are the three s135(1) thresholds?
recall.a: Net worth ₹500 crore, turnover ₹1,000 crore or net profit ₹5 crore.

recall.q: What is the penalty under s135(7)?
recall.a: Twice the amount that should have been transferred or ₹1 crore, whichever is less; officers one tenth or ₹2 lakh.

recall.q: What did the 2020 FCRA amendment do to administrative expenses?
recall.a: Capped them at 20 per cent, down from 50.

recall.q: What share of CSR in 2022-23 went to education and health together?
recall.a: More than half, ₹10,086 crore and ₹6,831 crore of ₹29,988 crore.

recall.q: What deductions does s133 give?
recall.a: 100 per cent for listed funds and 50 per cent for approved non-profits, with caps and a cash limit.

sections.title: Effective altruism and its critics
sections.big_idea: Effective altruism asks how to do the **most good per rupee**, and cost-per-life figures are model outputs to use with local data and judgement.
in_plain_words: Singer's 1972 essay argued that distance does not change a duty to prevent suffering. Effective altruism, named in 2011, added a second question: compare options and fund the most cost-effective. GiveWell estimates the good each donation does, publishes its models and treats overhead as a cost judged by what it buys.

A figure such as US$4,000 per life saved combines trial effects, local burden, coverage and costs, and its danger is false precision. It leaves out rights, dignity and long-run effects on the state. Critics point to incrementalism, elitism, uncounted harms, concentration among a few donors and longtermism. **Use cost-effectiveness beside participation and judgement**, and with local inputs in South Asia.

worked_example.title: How many lives does a budget buy?
worked_example.setup: Use GiveWell's September 2025 estimates of cost per life saved: US$4,000, US$5,500, US$3,500 and US$4,500. A funder has US$100,000. The figures are model estimates with wide uncertainty.
steps: Report the range of about 18 to 29, because the inputs are uncertain.
worked_example.answer: Roughly 18 to 29 lives depending on the charity, and the spread is smaller than the uncertainty in each estimate.

Importing a Sahel malaria figure into an Odisha district without local data.
Ignoring overlap with public schemes such as the National Health Mission.
Assuming outcomes that are hard to count, such as voice and dignity, do not matter.

recall.q: Who founded GiveWell and when?
recall.a: Holden Karnofsky and Elie Hassenfeld, in 2007.

recall.q: What does "cost per life saved" combine?
recall.a: Effect sizes from trials, local burden, coverage, costs and adjustments for what would have happened anyway.

recall.q: Name three of the five criticisms of effective altruism.
recall.a: Any three of: incrementalism, elitism, uncounted harms, concentration, longtermism.

recall.q: What does the deck say effective-giving thinking needs in South Asia?
recall.a: Local inputs: unit costs, disease burden and existing public provision.

recall.q: What question does trust-based philanthropy ask instead?
recall.a: How funders can share power with grantees.

sections.title: Power, trust and localisation
sections.big_idea: In every grant the **funder can leave at no cost**, so trust-based practice and localisation try to shift power, and the FCRA limits both in India.
in_plain_words: Every grant links unequal parties. The funder holds money, timing and the reporting template, while the grantee holds local knowledge and relationships. Trust-based philanthropy, set out in 2014, asks funders to share power through six practices, such as multi-year unrestricted funding and simpler paperwork. Restricted money leaves NGOs with no reserves, so one late payment stops work.

The Grand Bargain set a 25 per cent target for direct funding to local responders by 2020, and the reality in 2025 was 5 per cent. In India, section 7 of the FCRA forbids passing foreign money to another organisation, so **domestic philanthropy and CSR are the funds that can reach small groups**. Decolonising aid adds questions about who owns the data and the story.

key_terms.meaning: Treating grantees as partners and sharing decisions with them.
Money that pays only for named activities.
Money for whatever the organisation judges most needed.
2016 humanitarian deal with 51 commitments and 71 signatories.
Passing money and decisions to local and national actors.
Challenging who holds decisions, knowledge and money.

worked_example.title: Why a reserve matters, and the localisation gap
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: an NGO has a ₹2 crore yearly budget, equal to 200 lakh, and no unrestricted income. The Grand Bargain target is 25 per cent and the 2025 reality was 5 per cent.
steps: Three months of the budget: 200 ÷ 4 = 50 lakh.
With no reserve, a three-month funding delay cannot be covered, and a ₹50 lakh reserve would cover it.
Localisation gap in points: 25 − 5 = 20.
The gap is five times the actual share: 25 ÷ 5 = 5.
worked_example.answer: A ₹50 lakh reserve covers a three-month delay, and the localisation target is 20 points above where funding stands.

mistakes: Reading trust-based philanthropy as no accountability. The deck names weak accountability as its main risk.
Counting money passed through intermediaries as direct funding to local actors.
Planning for a sub-grant of foreign funds to a district partner, which s7 forbids.
Keeping all money restricted, which leaves no reserves, no learning and underpaid finance staff.

recall.q: Who set out trust-based philanthropy and when?
recall.a: The Whitman Institute in San Francisco, in 2014.

recall.q: Name three of the six practices.
recall.a: Any three of: multi-year unrestricted funding, do the homework, simplify paperwork, be transparent and responsive, solicit and act on feedback, offer support beyond the cheque.

recall.q: What was the Grand Bargain localisation target?
recall.a: At least 25 per cent of humanitarian funding to local and national responders by 2020.

recall.q: How much did local and national actors receive as first-tier recipients in 2025?
recall.a: 5 per cent, US$1.2 billion.

recall.q: Which money can still reach small Indian organisations?
recall.a: Domestic philanthropy and CSR.

sections.title: Putting it to work
sections.big_idea: Read the funder, read the terms before the amount, and **run the checklist** before you sign any grant.
in_plain_words: Before you apply, read a funder as carefully as it will read you. Six questions cover where its money comes from, what it funds and for how long, who decides, what it asks in return, how it behaved in 2020 and 2025, and whether it funds overhead. Public documents answer most of them, including the CSR policy, annual reports and MCA data.

A decision table scores seven terms as green, amber or red, and two or more reds is a reason to negotiate. The two worked cases show the rules at work: a CSR grant must fit Schedule VII, the implementing agency rules and the unspent-money rules, while a foreign grant must arrive in the FCRA account, respect the 20 per cent cap and avoid transfers. **Keep the completed checklist** with the signed agreement.

left.title: A CSR grant
items: Fit Schedule VII and local preference
Agency registered with MCA, with track record
Unspent money goes to a CSR account

right.title: A foreign grant
items: Arrives only in the FCRA account
Administrative cost at most 20 per cent
No transfer of funds to partners
Pay costs directly or fund from domestic money

key_terms.meaning: A one-page yearly note on a funder's size, priorities and stability.
Test for seven grant terms such as duration and overhead.
The NGO that carries out a CSR project under rule 4.
A multi-year project whose unspent CSR money goes to a special account.
Costs capped at 20 per cent for foreign contributions.
Ten checks to run before signing a grant agreement.

worked_example.title: Run the CSR grant and the FCRA budget
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's illustrative cases. A company has average net profits of ₹300 crore and offers ₹1.2 crore over two years. A European foundation offers an FCRA-registered NGO ₹1 crore, equal to 100 lakh, for one year.
steps: Company obligation: 300 × 2 ÷ 100 = 6 crore.
Your grant as a share of the obligation: 1.2 ÷ 6 = 20%.
Per year of the two-year grant: 1.2 ÷ 2 = 0.6 crore.
FCRA administrative cap: 100 × 20 ÷ 100 = 20 lakh.
Left for programme costs: 100 − 20 = 80 lakh.
worked_example.answer: The company must spend ₹6 crore, your grant is 20 per cent of it, and the foreign grant allows at most ₹20 lakh for administration, leaving ₹80 lakh.

mistakes: Reading the amount before the terms, when overhead and payment timing can turn a large grant into a loss.
Relying on rule 4(1)(d) as written, when it names 1961 Act sections replaced from 1 April 2026.
Budgeting an FCRA grant without checking how the Rules define administrative expenses.
Letting one funder supply more than half the income without a plan.

recall.q: What do green, amber and red tell you in the decision table?
recall.a: How good each of seven terms is: duration, restriction, overhead, reporting, data and IP, exit and payment.

recall.q: When is an impact assessment required under rule 8(3)?
recall.a: When the average obligation is ₹10 crore or more, for projects of ₹1 crore or more.

recall.q: Where must foreign contributions be received?
recall.a: In the FCRA account at the notified SBI branch in New Delhi.

recall.q: Name two of the six funder questions.
recall.a: Any two of: source of money, what and how long it funds, who decides, what it asks in return, 2020 and 2025 behaviour, overhead.

recall.q: Which data law does the checklist mention?
recall.a: The DPDP Act 2023, in relation to the funder's use of data.

notes.2: Read the agenda as a route from definitions to money to law. Sections 1 to 4 cover what aid is and the arguments around it, sections 5 and 6 the 2025 cuts and South Asian numbers, section 7 India, sections 8 to 10 **philanthropy, law and power**, and section 11 puts it to work.
notes.4: See first that one project can sit on five funding streams at once, each with its own rules, reporting and idea of success. Keep the two streams apart: **official aid is government money**, and private philanthropy comes from individuals, families, foundations and companies.
notes.5: Memorise the three tests: official, developmental, concessional. A flow must pass all three and go to a country on the DAC list or a multilateral agency. That is why **a large private foundation grant is not ODA**. The DAC adopted the concept in 1969 and it remains the standard measure.
notes.6: Use the table to sort flows quickly. Military aid and near-market loans fall into other official flows. Loan thresholds since 2018 are 45, 15 and 10 per cent grant element by income group. Refugee costs in the donor country count within limits, which is why **critics call the total inflated**.
notes.7: A loan now counts at its grant equivalent, recorded when it is agreed, so a 40 per cent grant element on US$100 million counts as US$40 million. Repayments no longer reduce ODA later. Headline reporting changed in 2019, so **compare totals across that break with care**.
notes.8: The 0.7 per cent figure comes from a 1970 UN resolution and was a political compromise with no estimate of need. Sweden and the Netherlands first met it in 1974. When a government announces a cut to 0.5 or 0.3 per cent, it **measures itself against that benchmark**.
notes.9: Only four of 34 DAC members met 0.7 in 2025: Norway, Luxembourg, Sweden and Denmark. The DAC as a whole gave 0.26, little more than a third of the target. A share of GNI rewards small generous economies, so **pair it with volume** on the next slide.
notes.10: Volume tells a different story from effort. Germany became the largest provider, just ahead of the United States, whose ODA fell 56.9 per cent. All five of the largest providers cut aid, **a first**, and made up 95.7 per cent of the decline. Totals stay preliminary until December 2026.
notes.11: Run four checks before quoting any aid number: gross or net, current or constant prices, flows or grant equivalent, preliminary or final. Then write the definition beside the number. **"Net ODA received, current US$, World Bank WDI 2023" is a citation**, while "aid to India" is not.
notes.13: Bilateral aid lets the donor choose country, sector and partner. Multilateral aid goes to a board that allocates by formula and need, so donors give up control and gain scale. Watch the hybrid: **multi-bi aid** passes through a UN agency but stays earmarked.
notes.14: Humanitarian aid saves lives in weeks and months, while development aid works over years, on different rules, staff and budgets. Both fell in 2025: humanitarian ODA by 35.8 per cent and bilateral core development by 26.3. The **nexus** tries to join relief to recovery.
notes.15: Match each form to who controls spending. Budget support gives the recipient government the most control and taxpayers the least visibility, which is why donors often prefer project aid. National NGOs mostly meet project grants, while **ministries meet loans, budget support and technical assistance**.
notes.16: Tied aid forces spending on goods and services from the donor, turning part of an aid budget into an export subsidy. Ask of any offer whether you must buy from the donor's suppliers or hire its consultants. **That answer changes the real value of the grant.**
notes.17: Follow the money down five layers: treasury, agency, UN agency or INGO, national NGO, community group. Each takes overhead and holds power over the next. Two thirds of humanitarian funding, US$17.4 billion, **could not be tracked past the first recipient**.
notes.18: ODA is one flow among several, and for many South Asian economies it is now small beside remittances, investment and commercial loans. The table tests each flow on official, concessional and counted. India's South-South cooperation **sits outside ODA** because India is not a DAC member.
notes.19: Aid follows donor priorities, and Ukraine in 2025 shows it: US$44.9 billion, more than bilateral ODA from DAC members to all least developed countries combined. Security and proximity shape allocation as much as poverty. Read a donor's country strategy for **what competes for the same budget line**.
notes.21: Keep four questions apart: does aid raise growth across countries, does this intervention work, does aid change accountability between state and citizens, and do rich people owe a duty to give. A programme can succeed on the second while **the first stays unanswered**.
notes.22: Sachs argued for a coordinated big push: very poor countries sit below the bottom rung, and a large injection of investment lets them climb. He asked aid to rise from US$65 billion in 2002 to between 135 and 195 billion by 2015. Remember his doctor image: **diagnose before prescribing**.
notes.23: Easterly's contrast is planners against searchers. Planners set large goals from outside and answer to no one. Searchers test small things, listen to users and are punished for failure. He accepted that some targeted health programmes work, so **his target is top-down planning**.
notes.24: Moyo separated humanitarian relief from ODA and argued that government-to-government aid reduces a state's need to tax and answer to citizens. Reviewers faulted her use of evidence and noted that Bauer and Easterly had made similar points earlier, with more nuance. **Test the argument against cases you know.**
notes.25: Use the table to find where the real disagreement lies. All three call poverty urgent and aid often wasted. They differ on the binding constraint: too little capital for Sachs, bad incentives for Easterly, aid dependence for Moyo. **Each prescription follows from its diagnosis.**
notes.26: Cross-country evidence swings with the method. Burnside and Dollar found aid works under good policy, Easterly, Levine and Roodman found that result gone with updated data, and Rajan and Subramanian found little effect either way. **Macro results are fragile**, so judge programmes by their own evaluations.
notes.27: Singer's drowning child makes the ethical case: if you can prevent something very bad without sacrificing anything of comparable importance, you ought to, and distance makes no moral difference. He wrote it in 1971 for refugees from the Bangladesh war, so the **argument behind effective altruism began in South Asia**.
notes.28: Take a test from each side. From Sachs: some problems need scale and coordination, and under-funding a proven programme costs lives. From Easterly and Moyo: build feedback from the people served and ask who is accountable. **Write down which question your programme answers.**
notes.30: Read the table as a ten-year sequence: Monterrey 2002, Rome 2003, Paris 2005, Accra 2008, Busan 2011. Each forum asked how aid should be delivered as well as how much. Paris is the one to know best, with **five principles and 12 indicators**.
notes.31: Learn the five Paris principles in order: ownership, alignment, harmonisation, results, mutual accountability. Each answers a complaint from recipient governments about too many donors with their own systems, plans and missions. Harmonisation means joint missions and **fewer parallel project units** that bypass ministries.
notes.32: The 2010 monitoring found progress that was real but slow, with most targets missed. Only coordinated technical cooperation was met. The pattern: **targets that depended on recipients improved more** than those needing donors to change procedures. Look at parallel units: 1,158 against a target of 565.
notes.33: Accra added three areas: ownership with wider participation, inclusive partnerships and delivering results, plus more predictable aid so governments can plan beyond a single year. Its most visible shift was recognising that **civil society and parliaments, as well as governments**, shape development policy.
notes.34: Busan widened the frame from aid effectiveness to development effectiveness, bringing in the private sector, civil society, parliamentarians and local authorities. It set four principles and created the Global Partnership, which replaced the forum process. The last principle is accountability **to each other, to beneficiaries and to citizens**.
notes.35: Use the two sketches to judge ownership in a ministry: how many parallel project units, how much aid appears in the budget, how many separate missions. Remember the caution: a government that does not answer to its citizens can claim ownership too, which **Accra's addition of parliaments** was meant to address.
notes.36: Six forces stalled the agenda, from donor logos and shared risk to attribution, politics and fragmentation. Then the 2025 cuts reduced the money itself. For a South Asian NGO the principles still work as a checklist: **a funder who aligns with your plan, accepts your systems and reports jointly** is following Paris.
notes.38: The 2025 fall of 23.1 per cent in real terms is the largest on record and returns aid to 2015 levels. Hold two truths: it is concentrated, since the US cut 56.9 per cent, and it is broad, since **26 members cut and only eight held or increased**. The OECD projects a further 5.8 per cent fall in 2026.
notes.39: Follow the dates. The order of 20 January paused aid, 10 March saw 83 per cent of programmes announced as cancelled, and USAID stopped implementing on 1 July. The slide adds a legal point: because Congress reorganised USAID in 1998, **only an act of Congress can formally abolish it**.
notes.40: The order's operative section froze new obligations and disbursements for 90 days while programmes were reviewed against foreign policy goals. For implementers, a pause stops salaries, supply chains and services within weeks, even if a programme is later restored. **Several lawsuits challenged the power** to do this without Congress.
notes.41: The UK wrote 0.7 into law in 2015, cut to 0.5 in 2021, and announced 0.3 per cent for 2027 to fund defence. It is still the third largest provider at US$17.2 billion. Aid budgets across donors are moving to defence and security, so **check current FCDO country allocations** before assuming a programme continues.
notes.42: All five of the largest providers cut aid in the same year, a first. Germany led because US aid fell so far. The DAC Chair attributed smaller donors' cuts to budget, security and political pressure. Remember the other half of the picture: **only four donors exceeded 0.7 per cent**.
notes.43: The Lancet study estimates 91.8 million deaths prevented by USAID funding from 2001 to 2021 and 14.05 million extra deaths by 2030 if the cuts continue, with a range of 8.5 to 19.7 million. It is observational with wide intervals, so **give the range and say it is an association**.
notes.44: Cuts fall hardest where alternatives are fewest: down 25.8 per cent for least developed countries and 35.8 for humanitarian ODA. Gender-related aid was already falling before 2025, down 13 per cent from 2023 to 2024. Use the table to **describe which sectors and places** your funders have cut.
notes.45: Many South Asian NGOs never held a USAID contract and felt the cut as a stop-work notice from a partner. Indian groups face an extra limit: FCRA funds cannot be passed on, so a larger partner cannot rescue them. Build **funder diversity, reserves of three to six months and exit clauses**.
notes.47: Compare three measures for each country, since they tell three stories: total, share of national income and amount per person. Bangladesh receives the most in total, Afghanistan the highest share of GNI at 17.76 per cent, and India the least per person at US$1.65. **Net means repayments are subtracted.**
notes.48: Totals jump because loans are disbursed in lumps and repayments return in other years. Bangladesh shows the clearest rise, from US$2.15 billion in 2012 to US$5.68 billion in 2023, while India stays between about US$1.7 and 3.2 billion. **Read the trend across years.**
notes.49: India receives a lot of aid in absolute terms and depends on it very little: 0.07 per cent of GNI against 2.82 for Nepal, forty times larger. Dependence sets bargaining power, since a ministry that relies on donors has less room to refuse conditions. **Per person**, India got US$1.65 against Nepal's US$39.51.
notes.50: Ranking per person reverses the table: small countries get far more per head, and India, the most populous, gets the least. Sri Lanka's figure moved from US$0.55 in 2022 to US$37.54 in 2023, so **show more than one year** before drawing a conclusion about any country.
notes.51: A negative net figure means repayments on earlier concessional loans exceeded new aid that year. Sri Lanka's 2018 figure of minus US$247 million tells you about loan timing and says nothing about donor goodwill. When you cite aid to a borrowing country, **state whether it is gross or net**.
notes.52: Nepal shows aid dependence: net ODA peaked at US$1.76 billion in 2020, 5.2 per cent of GNI, and fell to 2.82 per cent by 2023. When aid is a large share of public investment, donor timing shapes what the state can build. **Track multi-year commitments** as closely as the national budget.
notes.53: Afghanistan is the outlier: aid equalled 33.4 per cent of GNI in 2012 and 17.76 in 2023. When aid supplies a third of income, aid decisions are economic policy and a donor exit is an economic shock. The slide advises treating **the level as indicative and the direction as the finding**.
notes.54: Bangladesh's net ODA more than doubled between 2012 and 2023, and per person from US$13.89 to 33.15, while its share of GNI stayed between about 0.9 and 1.6 per cent. Rising totals can mean more borrowing as well as more grants, so **read the debt data alongside**.
notes.56: India is both recipient and provider. It receives US$2.38 billion in net ODA and also gives development finance and training through the MEA, outside DAC totals and under its own rules. It frames this as **South-South cooperation**, which avoids the donor-recipient hierarchy.
notes.57: ITEC dates from 15 September 1964 and is demand-driven: partners ask for the training they want. India pays airfare, boarding and tuition for trainees in its institutions. The slide cites coverage of about 158 countries from MEA material. **Check itecgoi.in** for current course lists.
notes.58: The DPA was created inside the MEA in 2012 to bring outgoing assistance under one roof. Keeping it in the foreign ministry treats development partnership as foreign policy. For NGOs and researchers the consequence is **few formal routes in**, unlike DAC donors' open calls for proposals.
notes.59: IDEAS routes government-backed concessional lines of credit through Exim Bank, and they pay for goods and services from India. The scale: 300 plus lines, US$32 billion, 68 partner countries and about 600 projects. Credits let partner buyers **import from India on deferred terms**.
notes.60: Bangladesh takes about a quarter of the US$32 billion, and the neighbourhood has priority under Neighbourhood First. Africa received 196 lines worth US$12 billion across 42 countries. Treat the chart as **the geography of Indian lines of credit** as at August 2024.
notes.61: Hold two truths together. India's partnership is demand-driven with few policy conditions, and lines of credit buy Indian goods, which is close to the OECD definition of tied aid. Credits must be repaid and results data are limited. **Exim Bank itself invited impact assessments.**
notes.62: The table describes rules and channels and says nothing on its own about which model delivers more development. DAC donors report to the OECD and often attach conditions, while India does not report as ODA and attaches few. Procurement is the sharpest contrast: **mostly untied for DAC donors**, tied to India for lines of credit.
notes.64: Social sector funding is about ₹27 lakh crore in FY25, and about 95 per cent of it is public. Private philanthropy is ₹1.43 lakh crore against a gap near ₹16 lakh crore. The slide's lesson: **philanthropy cannot replace the state**, and its value is risk-taking, innovation, advocacy and filling gaps. Quote these as consultancy estimates.
notes.65: Families are at the centre of private giving, about 42 per cent, including through the CSR of family-run businesses, which provide 65 to 70 per cent of private-sector CSR. Family offices grew from 45 to 300 between 2018 and 2024. Causes are **widening** to gender, climate, livelihoods, arts and animal welfare.
notes.66: Section 135 applies when any one of three thresholds was met in the preceding financial year: net worth ₹500 crore, turnover ₹1,000 crore or net profit ₹5 crore. A CSR committee of three or more directors, one independent, drafts the policy. The Board does the work itself if the spend is **₹50 lakh or less**.
notes.67: Run the 2 per cent rule as four steps: calculate on three years' average net profit, spend in the year, move unspent money for ongoing projects to the Unspent CSR Account within 30 days, and send other unspent money to a Schedule VII fund. The penalty is **twice the amount or ₹1 crore, whichever is less**.
notes.68: CSR counts only if it falls within Schedule VII, so check each activity against the list before agreeing a project. Education, health, livelihoods and the environment are the main items. Benefits to the company's own employees do not count, and **activities outside India count only for training Indian sports personnel**.
notes.69: Reported CSR rose from ₹20,218 crore in 2018-19 to ₹29,988 crore in 2022-23, in every year including the pandemic. It is a large but minority share of private giving. These are **reported figures**, and the state-level series ends in 2022-23.
notes.70: CSR follows company headquarters. Maharashtra got ₹5,497 crore in 2022-23, Bihar ₹235 crore and Meghalaya ₹22 crore, and ₹6,061 crore was labelled PAN India with no state. Education and health took **more than half**. Read local preference in s135(5) with this concentration in mind.
notes.71: FCRA regulates foreign contributions: registration or prior permission is needed, funds must be used for the stated purpose, registration must be renewed, and it can be suspended or cancelled. Certain people cannot accept at all. **FCRA status is the first thing a foreign funder will ask** an Indian partner.
notes.72: Learn the 2020 changes by section: s7 bars transfers to any other person, s8 caps administrative expenses at 20 per cent (down from 50), s17 requires receipt in an FCRA account at a notified SBI branch in New Delhi, and s12A requires Aadhaar of office bearers. **The Supreme Court upheld** the main amendments in Noel Harper.
notes.73: From 1 April 2026 section 133 of the Income-tax Act 2025 governs donation deductions, taking the role of section 80G. Know the two rates: 100 per cent for listed funds and 50 per cent for approved charities. **Cash over ₹2,000 earns no deduction**, and CSR sums paid into some funds do not qualify.
notes.75: Follow Singer's chain: suffering is bad, prevent it if the moral cost is small, distance does not change the duty. Effective altruism, named in 2011, adds a second question: how do you do the most good per rupee? It measures **outcomes per dollar** and asks donors to give a meaningful share by evidence.
notes.76: GiveWell estimates how much good a donation does, using published evidence and its own models, and treats overhead as a cost judged by what it buys. It publishes its reasoning. Its rapid response fund disbursed US$39 million in 2025. Leif Wenar criticises it for **under-counting harms** of recommended charities.
notes.77: Read the unit cost and cost per life saved for the four top charities: US$4,000, US$5,500, US$3,500 and US$4,500. They are model estimates with wide uncertainty, for sub-Saharan African settings. **Do not copy them into a proposal** for an Indian district without local data.
notes.78: A figure such as US$4,000 per life saved is model output, and its main danger is false precision. It helps compare options on the same method. It leaves out rights, dignity, voice and long-run effects. Ask **which inputs drive the result**, whether the estimate travels, and who chose the outcome counted.
notes.79: Learn five criticisms: incrementalism, elitism, uncounted harms, concentration among a few large donors, and longtermism. The slide closes sensibly: cost-effectiveness stays useful, and the criticisms are reasons to use it **beside participation and judgement**. Many arose after the FTX collapse.
notes.80: Effective giving needs local inputs, because unit costs, disease burden and existing public provision differ from the settings GiveWell models. Compare two ways of reaching the same goal, price them with local costs and count the counterfactual. The Jharkhand anaemia example shows **the habit in a sentence**.
notes.81: Place the two cultures side by side. Effective altruism asks where a dollar does most good and the funder decides using evidence. Trust-based philanthropy asks how funders can share power, with multi-year unrestricted money. Each has a main risk: **ignoring what cannot be counted**, or weak accountability.
notes.83: Every grant is a relationship between unequal parties. The funder holds money, timing, indicators and the power to leave, while the grantee holds local knowledge and relationships. The slide's test: **who can end the relationship at short notice without cost?** In most grants it is the funder alone.
notes.84: Trust-based philanthropy, set out in 2014 by the Whitman Institute, treats grantees as partners and reduces funder burdens. It spread during COVID-19 when funders relaxed reporting. The hardest problem the slide names is **keeping meaningful measurement while cutting reporting**.
notes.85: Use the six practices as a checklist for any funder, including a CSR team: multi-year unrestricted funding, do the homework, simplify paperwork, be transparent, act on feedback, and support beyond the cheque. **Each moves a burden from grantee to funder.**
notes.86: Restricted money pays only for named activities, and most Indian NGOs live on it. With no reserves, one late payment stops work. In the illustrative case a ₹2 crore NGO cannot cover a three-month delay, while a **₹50 lakh reserve would**. Foreign funds add the 20 per cent administrative cap.
notes.87: At the 2016 World Humanitarian Summit, donors and agencies agreed the Grand Bargain: 51 commitments, now 71 signatories. The localisation target is at least 25 per cent of humanitarian funding to local and national responders by 2020, as directly as possible. It was **revised in 2021 and 2023**.
notes.88: Target 25 per cent, reality 5 per cent: local and national actors received US$1.2 billion in 2025 as first-tier recipients. Counting money passed on through intermediaries, 8.7 per cent, down from 9.5. The gap is partly counting and partly power, because **intermediaries keep control**.
notes.89: Since 2020, s7 of the FCRA stops a registered organisation passing foreign funds to anyone else, so an international NGO's Indian office cannot sub-grant to a district partner. Foreign funders must contract each organisation directly, which favours larger NGOs. **Domestic philanthropy and CSR can still reach small groups.**
notes.90: Decolonising aid asks who holds decisions, knowledge and money. Use the six questions as an audit of any proposal, including by Indian funders working in other states: whose definition of the problem, who owns the data, who is named author, how much is spent locally, who decides when it ends, and **whether local staff are paid equally**.
notes.92: Read the funder as carefully as it will read you. The six questions cover its source of money, what it funds and for how long, who decides, what it asks in return, how it behaved in 2020 and 2025, and overhead. **Ask two current grantees** what it is like, which tells you more than the website.
notes.93: Public sources show a funder's size, priorities and stability before the first meeting: the CSR policy on the company website (s135(4)), the annual CSR report, MCA data, OECD data, foundation annual reports and the India Philanthropy Report. Keep **a one-page funder profile** for each and update it yearly.
notes.94: Read terms before the amount. Seven terms decide whether a grant strengthens or drains an organisation, each with a green, amber and red test. **Two or more reds is a reason to negotiate.** Under-priced overhead and payment in arrears together can turn a large grant into a loss.
notes.95: Work the case in order: compute the obligation (2 per cent of average net profit), test eligibility under Schedule VII, check local preference, then your standing as an implementing agency. Note the caution that rule 4(1)(d) still names **1961 Act sections** the 2025 Act replaced. Negotiate overhead, advance payment and data ownership.
notes.96: Plan the budget against the FCRA before signing. The four steps: receive in the FCRA account, cap administrative expenses at 20 per cent, send nothing on to the three community groups, then redesign. Option A is **direct delivery by your staff**, and option B is direct funding of the groups or domestic money for their share.
notes.97: Run these ten checks with your finance lead and a board member before signing, and keep the completed list with the agreement as a record of what you knew. The last check asks whether one funder supplies more than half your income, which **limits your ability to refuse terms**.
notes.98: Treat this as a self-test: can you say each point in a sentence? The last point asks you to recheck the OECD figures when final 2025 data arrive in December 2026. Facts are stated as of October 2026, so **check for later amendments** and new data before you quote.
notes.99: Use this list to choose your next course by need: Development Finance 101 for the money, CSR & ESG 101 for company giving, Fundraising Basics 101 if you are writing a proposal this month, Cost Effectiveness 101 for comparing options. **The deck says all courses are free.**
